Compute - CUDA Core

REAL TASK · 1 / 4
  • Task: a steel plate with a hole, pulled by 800 N — will it hold?
  • Model: elastic steel (E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3, yield 250 MPa).
  • Objective: peak stress — no closed form for this finite plate, solve numerically.
  • Principle: chop into 768 triangles; each is a small spring (CST element).
  • Solve: 850 unknown displacements, 460 coupled solver passes.
  • Naïve: one CPU thread works through all of it strictly in order.
  • Kernel: one thread per triangle — 768 threads in one launch.
  • CUDA cores: thousands of units execute the same formulas on different corners at once.
  • Uniform: same instructions, different data — triangles never wait on each other.
  • Output: von Mises stress per triangle — hotspot at the hole flanks.
  • Peak: 20.4 MPa = 2.04× the 10 MPa nominal (handbook: 2.16).
  • Verdict: 12× margin: 20.4 MPa vs 250 MPa yield.
  • The plate becomes triangles; each triangle acts as a spring.
Original CST plane-stress computation · Kt cf. Peterson’s Stress Concentration Factors

Compute - CUDA Core

REAL TASK · 1 / 4
  • Zoom: the hottest triangle at the hole flank — 0.234 mm².
  • Known: corner displacements u from the solver, in µm.
  • Goal: stress inside, from u via B and D.
  • Slow way: one worker chains u→ε→σ→vM for triangle 0, 1, 2 … 768.
  • Each pass: ≈30 multiplies/adds on that triangle’s nine numbers.
  • Independent: only its own corners — no triangle waits on another.
  • Every core: same chain, different triangle: ε = B·u, σ = D·ε.
  • Strain: εy = 0.1826×1.5708 + 0.7661×1.7057 − 0.9487×1.5714 ≈ 102.7 µε
  • Result: 20.74 MPa → vM 20.43 MPa.
  • Output: stress for every triangle at once — the full stress map.
  • Flank: 20.43 MPa = 2.04× the 10 MPa far-field.
  • Margin: yield 250 MPa → 12× safety factor.
  • Zoom: the hottest triangle, three corners, nine numbers.
Original CST plane-stress computation · CUDA programming model: NVIDIA CUDA Programming Guide

Compute - Tensor Core

WORKLOAD · 1 / 3
  • A user types “The capital of France is”.
  • Our large language model (LLM) must choose the next piece of text.
  • A token is a text piece; “Paris” is our example completion.
PROMPT

The capital of France is

Paris ← next token
Token = a piece of text
  • The model converts the prompt into numbers called input activations.
  • Learned numbers, called weights, determine how a layer combines those inputs.
  • A matrix arranges these numbers into rows and columns.
Input activations
Weight matrix
Output activations
  • The layer receives input matrix A, weight matrix B, and starting totals C.
  • Tensor Cores multiply blocks of A and B and add C.
  • Output D supplies new numbers to the model’s next computation.
D = A × B + C
  • The model computes scores for possible next tokens.

Compute - SFU

WORKLOAD · 1 / 1
  • Prompt: “The capital of France is” (five candidates)
  • SFU functions: 1/x, √x, 1/√x, eˣ, log₂x, sin, cos
  • In an LLM: softmax eˣ; LayerNorm, RMSNorm 1/√variance; activations (GELU, sigmoid) eˣ; RoPE sin, cos
  • Softmax turns scores into probabilities; the SFU’s eˣ makes it fast.

Compute - DPX

WORKLOAD · 1 / 2
  • Task: align each phoneme to the audio frames it spans — forced alignment.
  • Used in: TTS duration labels, ASR timing, subtitles, pronunciation scoring.
  • Objective: the best path that consumes phonemes and frames in order.

Synthesized speech; word boundaries measured, phoneme split illustrative

  • Score every phoneme × frame pair in a table.
  • Each cell extends the best route — diagonal (both advance), up (frame stretches a sound), left (phoneme moves on).
  • The best path to the far corner is the alignment.
Diagonal
phoneme + frame advance
Up
frame stretches a sound
Left
phoneme moves on
  • Phonemes align to speech frames, one table cell at a time.
Illustration · Hopper guide · sources in notes

Compute - DPX

WORKLOAD · 1 / 2
  • Each cell of the phoneme × frame table repeats one small decision.
  • A few integer adds and a max pick how the alignment extends.
  • The path reaching the far corner is the alignment.
  • DPX folds a cell’s adds + max into a single instruction.
  • Longer audio and richer phone sets scale the table into the millions.
  • Genomics, speech, and DTW share this repeated best-of-few pattern.
Cell decision
adds + max
DPX instruction
several ops at once
Alignment table
millions of cells
  • Each cell is a best-of-few choice, made millions of times.

Graphics Rendering - Rasterizer

FROM TRIANGLES TO PIXELS · 1 / 2
  • Our simulation has updated the positions of its objects.
  • We now need an image from a chosen camera viewpoint.
  • The application sends surface triangles and the camera settings into the graphics pipeline.
  • A triangle is a surface patch with three corners.
  • Earlier stages project its corners onto the screen.
  • The rasterizer finds which screen locations that projected triangle covers, ready for coloring.
  • A pixel is one image cell; a sample is a tested location within it.
  • A fragment carries a candidate color contribution and coverage for later tests.
  • Drag the corners to change which samples are covered.
Illustration · teaching example · sources in notes

Graphics Rendering - Texture Unit

WORKLOAD · 1 / 2
  • A texture is spatially varying surface data.
  • The surface reads it via texture coordinates; one stored value is a texel.
  • Common texture maps:
  • Base color / albedo — surface color or pattern.
  • Roughness — matte vs glossy.
  • Metallic — metal or dielectric (plastic/wood).
  • Normal — fakes micro-detail (scratches, pores, weave, grain) without geometry.
  • Height / displacement — surface bumps and grooves.
  • Opacity / alpha — transparency or cutouts.
  • Ambient occlusion — small-scale shadowing.
  • Emission — areas that emit light.
  • Specular — reflection strength (some material models).
  • Our surface requests a value between four stored texels.
  • The point lies 25% across and 60% down their neighborhood.
  • Bilinear filtering mixes all four values; closer texels receive more weight.
  • Texture maps store one surface property per image channel.
glTF 2.0 material model · sources in notes

Graphics Rendering - ROP

WORKLOAD · 1 / 2
  • A red ball sits in front of a blue box; both cover the same screen location.
  • Draw the opaque blue box first.
  • The ball’s alpha is 0.3: blend 30% red with 70% of the existing blue.
  • The framebuffer holds the resulting image and depth data.
  • Depth records which surface is nearer; smaller wins here.
  • Red 0.40 passes against blue 0.60; farther red fails.
  • Blend the passing red: 0.3 × red + 0.7 × blue.
  • Passing red: alpha 0 shows blue; alpha 1 shows red.
  • ROP output operations test and blend fragments after projection.
Illustration · teaching example · sources in notes

Graphics Rendering - ROP

WORKLOAD · 1 / 2
  • Show our ball-and-box scene only through a portal opening.
  • Stencil stores an integer mask at each screen pixel.
  • Mark the opening 1 and everything outside it 0.
  • Draw the scene only where the stored value is 1.
  • The same scene still covers pixels outside the portal.
  • For each candidate fragment, test whether its stencil value equals 1.
  • Toggle the mask: outside fragments are blocked when the test is enabled.
Mask disabled: whole scene visible.
  • ROP stencil testing restricts where this rendering pass writes.
Illustration · teaching example · sources in notes

Graphics Rendering - RT Core

EXPENSIVE APPROACH · 1 / 2
  • A shiny car must reflect its scene in real time.
  • The scene is triangles: millions of them.
  • Each pixel fires a ray; reflections fire more.
  • Naïvely, every ray tests against every triangle: O(N × M).
  • A BVH (bounding volume hierarchy) nests boxes around triangle groups.
  • The typical search per ray drops toward O(log M).
  • Intuition, not a worst-case guarantee.
  • Naïve ray tracing tests N rays against M triangles — O(N × M) work.
NVIDIA · Turing architecture · sources in notes

Graphics Rendering - RT Core

ONE RAY, ONE QUESTION · 1 / 2
  • One camera ray crosses the scene and strikes the car's hood.
  • The question: which of the scene's millions of triangles is hit first?
  • Answering that is the RT Core's only job.
  • Layer by layer: hit a box, descend, ignore the rest.
  • Bottom layer: exact triangle tests — smallest positive t wins.
Ready: start at the root.
  • RT Cores accelerate the search for what a ray intersects; BVH lets them skip most scene geometry.
NVIDIA · Turing architecture · sources in notes

Media Process - NVENC/NVDEC

WORKLOAD · 1 / 2
  • A 1280×720 CCTV camera at 30 FPS fills a network fast.
  • Raw 8-bit YUV 4:2:0 video costs about 1.5 bytes per pixel.
  • That is roughly 2.5 GB every minute for a single camera.
1280×720 × 30 × 1.5 B ≈ 2.5 GB/min
  • Encode the same camera as H.265 at 2 Mbps: about 15 MB per minute.
  • NVENC compresses on the sending side; NVDEC reconstructs frames on the receiving side.
  • A codec is the shared recipe both sides follow to compress and rebuild video.
Camera frames
NVENC
2 Mbps H.265 stream
NVDEC
Frames for processing
  • NVENC compresses for the network; NVDEC reconstructs for processing.
OpenCV · sample footage · sources in notes

Media Process - NVENC/NVDEC

WORKLOAD · 1 / 1
  • NVENC predicts the current frame from the previously reconstructed reference frame.
  • The frame is split into coding blocks; each searches the reference for its best match.
  • Residual = original − prediction, near-black where prediction succeeds.
  • Transmit motion plus a small residual — not the whole frame.
Zhang et al. · IEEE TP 2023 figure · sources in notes

Media Process - NVENC/NVDEC

WORKLOAD · 1 / 1
  • Predict each block from the previous frame.
  • Code only what prediction misses.
  • Only motion plus quantized residuals travel; both sides rebuild the reference identically.
NVIDIA Video Codec SDK · teaching flow · sources in notes

Media Process - OFA

WORKLOAD · 1 / 1
  • OFA reads two consecutive frames and returns dense per-pixel motion vectors.
  • Hardware finds where pixels moved; near-zero CPU cost.
  • Localize movement: strong vectors mark moving regions.
  • Stabilize: global shift estimates camera shake; counter-shift each frame.
  • Save work: static regions can be skipped downstream.
  • Vectors point where pixels moved; magnitude localizes motion, global shift reveals shake.
OpenCV · vtest.avi (PETS footage) · flow computed on the frames shown · sources in notes

Media Process - JPEG decode

NATURAL IMAGES ARE SMOOTH · 1 / 2
  • Natural images are locally smooth: neighboring pixels are highly correlated.
  • Within a small 8 × 8 block, values change gently instead of randomly.
  • That redundancy is exactly what a compressor can exploit.
  • A 2D DCT expresses each 8 × 8 block using cosine patterns of different horizontal and vertical spatial frequencies.
  • For natural images, most information is concentrated in a few low-frequency components,
  • while many high-frequency components are small.
  • Neighboring pixels in natural images are highly correlated.
Images · CS184 lec 22 slide 13 · reference visualization · sources in notes

Movement - TMA

WORKLOAD · 1 / 2
  • Our layer needs consecutive tiles without overwriting unfinished work.
  • Shared-memory buffer A holds tile 0; B is empty.
  • Compute A while TMA loads tile 1 into B.
  • TMA is mainly used for the data transfer between the HBM and SRAM.
Ready: A contains tile 0; B is empty.
  • Loading B can overlap with computing A.
Illustration · Hopper guide · sources in notes

Movement - Copy Engine

WORKLOAD · 1 / 2
  • A batch of model inputs sits in CPU memory.
  • The GPU needs that batch in its own memory before computation starts.
  • A Copy Engine transfers the batch; supported systems can also copy between GPUs. Sample applications in LLM training:
    • Data loading: training batches stream H2D from pinned host memory as async DMA, overlapped with compute.
    • Model-weight loading: weights stream H2D at startup, or from host memory when the model exceeds VRAM.
    • Activation offloading: checkpointing streams saved activations D2H and reloads them in backward, double-buffered to hide latency.
CPU memory
Application batch
Copy Engine
Bulk transfer
GPU memory
Ready batch
  • Copy Engines offload bulk transfers between memory domains.
